title: Definitions and conceptual analysis
note: A definition pairs a term (the definiendum) with words that give its meaning (the definiens). Lexical definitions report usage, stipulative ones assign a meaning, and precising ones sharpen a vague term. A good definition is neither too broad nor too narrow and is not circular. Conceptual analysis tests a proposed definition against real and imagined cases.

read.title: Testing a definition
text: Many disagreements turn on words. Before arguing whether something is fair, art, or free, it helps to ask what the word means. A definition pairs the term being defined, the definiendum, with words that give its meaning, the definiens.

Definitions do different jobs. A lexical definition reports how a word is already used, as a dictionary does. A stipulative definition assigns a meaning for present purposes. A precising definition sharpens a vague term, as a law might define 'adult' as anyone eighteen or older.

A proposed definition can be tested with cases. Try 'A bird is an animal that flies.' Bats fly but are not birds, so the definition is too broad. Penguins are birds but cannot fly, so it is also too narrow. A good definition fits all and only the things the term applies to. It also must not be circular: 'freedom is being free' teaches nothing.

This method of proposing definitions and testing them against cases, real or imagined, is conceptual analysis. Socrates practiced it when he asked what courage or justice is. A famous modern example: Edmund Gettier described cases of justified true belief that seem not to be knowledge, challenging a long-popular definition.

q.q: Why is 'A bird is an animal that flies' too broad?
o: Bats fly but are not birds

q.q: A law defining 'adult' as anyone eighteen or older gives what kind of definition?
